title: Book 15 — Athena summons Telemachus from Lacedaemon—he meets with Theoclymenus at Pylos and brings him to Ithaca—on landing he goes to the hut of Eumaeus
paragraphs: But Athena went to the beautiful city of Lacedaemon to tell Odysseus’s son that he must return home immediately. She found him and Pisistratus sleeping in the forecourt of Menelaus’s house. Pisistratus was fast asleep, but Telemachus couldn’t rest all night, thinking about his unhappy father. So Athena came close to him and said:

“Telemachus, you shouldn’t stay so far from home any longer, or leave your property with such dangerous people in your house. They’ll devour everything you own, and your journey will have been pointless. Ask Menelaus to send you home at once if you want to find your noble mother still there when you return. Her father and brothers are already urging her to marry Eurymachus, who has offered her more gifts than any of the others and keeps increasing his wedding presents. I hope nothing valuable has been taken from the house in spite of you, but you know how women are—they always want to do their best for the man who marries them, and never give another thought to the children of their first husband, or to their father once he’s dead and gone. Go home, therefore, and put everything in the care of the most trustworthy woman servant you have, until heaven sees fit to send you a wife of your own. Let me also tell you about another matter you had better attend to. The leading suitors are lying in wait for you in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, planning to kill you before you can reach home. I hardly think they’ll succeed—it’s more likely that some of those who are now devouring your property will find their own graves. Sail night and day, and keep your ship well away from the islands. The god who watches over and protects you will send you a fair wind. As soon as you reach Ithaca, send your ship and crew on to the town, but go straight to the swineherd who tends your pigs. He’s well disposed toward you—stay with him for the night, then send him to Penelope to tell her you’ve returned safely from Pylos.”
Then she returned to Olympus. But Telemachus stirred Pisistratus with his heel to wake him, saying, “Wake up, Pisistratus, and harness the horses to the chariot. We must head for home.”

But Pisistratus said, “No matter how urgent this is, we can’t drive in the dark. Morning will come soon. Wait until Menelaus brings his gifts and loads them in the chariot for us, and let him say goodbye properly. A guest should never forget a host who has shown him kindness, as long as he lives.”

As he spoke, dawn began to break, and Menelaus, who had already risen and left Helen in bed, came toward them. When Telemachus saw him, he quickly put on his shirt, threw a great cloak over his shoulders, and went out to meet him. “Menelaus,” he said, “let me return now to my own country, for I want to get home.”

Menelaus answered, “Telemachus, if you insist on leaving, I won’t detain you. I don’t like to see a host who’s either too clingy with his guests or too rude to them. Moderation is best in all things—not letting a man go when he wants to leave is as bad as telling him to go if he’d rather stay. A host should treat his guest well while he’s in the house and help him on his way when he wants to leave. Wait, then, until I can load your beautiful presents into your chariot, and until you’ve seen them yourself. I’ll tell the women to prepare a proper meal from what we have in the house. It will be both more fitting and more economical for you to eat before setting out on such a long journey. Moreover, if you’d like to tour Hellas or the Peloponnese, I’ll harness my horses and escort you personally through all our principal cities. No one will send us away empty-handed—everyone will give us something: a bronze tripod, a pair of mules, or a golden cup.”

“Menelaus,” replied Telemachus, “I want to go home at once. When I left, I abandoned my property without protection, and I’m afraid that while searching for my father, I’ll be ruined myself, or discover that something valuable has been stolen in my absence.”

When Menelaus heard this, he immediately told his wife and servants to prepare a proper meal from what was available in the house. At that moment Eteoneus joined him, since he lived nearby and had just gotten up. Menelaus told him to light the fire and cook some meat, which he did at once. Then Menelaus went down to his fragrant storeroom, not alone—Helen went too, along with Megapenthes. When he reached the place where his household treasures were kept, he selected a double cup and told his son Megapenthes to bring a silver mixing bowl as well. Meanwhile, Helen went to the chest where she kept the lovely dresses she had made with her own hands. She took out the largest and most beautifully embroidered one, which glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. Then they all returned through the house until they reached Telemachus, and Menelaus said, “Telemachus, may Zeus, Hera’s mighty husband, bring you safely home as you desire. I now present you with the finest and most precious piece of metalwork in all my house. It’s a mixing bowl of pure silver, except for the rim, which is inlaid with gold, and it’s the work of Hephaestus. King Phaedimus of the Sidonians gave it to me during a visit I paid him on my way home. I’d like to give it to you.”
With these words he placed the double cup in Telemachus’s hands, while Megapenthes brought the beautiful mixing bowl and set it before him. Nearby stood lovely Helen with the robe ready in her hands.

“I too, my son,” she said, “have something for you as a keepsake from my own hand—the hand of Helen. It’s for your bride to wear on her wedding day. Until then, have your dear mother keep it for you. May you return rejoicing to your own country and home.”

So saying, she gave him the robe, and he received it gladly. Then Pisistratus put the presents into the chariot, admiring them all as he did so. Presently Menelaus led Telemachus and Pisistratus into the house, where they both sat down to eat. A maid servant brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands. She drew a clean table beside them, and a senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house. Eteoneus carved the meat and gave them each their portions, while Megapenthes poured the wine. Then they helped themselves to the good food before them. But as soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus and Pisistratus harnessed the horses and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court, and Menelaus followed them with a golden goblet of wine in his right hand so they could make a drink offering before departing. He stood in front of the horses and toasted them, saying, “Farewell to both of you. Be sure to tell Nestor how I’ve treated you, for he was as kind to me as any father could be while we Achaeans were fighting before Troy.”

“We’ll certainly tell him everything as soon as we see him, sir,” answered Telemachus. “I wish I could be as certain of finding Odysseus returned when I get back to Ithaca, so I could tell him of your great kindness and of the many beautiful presents I’m taking with me.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew on his right—an eagle carrying a great white goose in its talons that it had snatched from the farmyard, while all the men and women ran after it, shouting. It came quite close to them and flew away on their right, in front of the horses. When they saw it, they were glad and took heart. At that Pisistratus said, “Tell me, Menelaus, has heaven sent this omen for us or for you?”

Menelaus was thinking what would be the most appropriate response, but Helen was quicker and said, “I’ll interpret this sign as heaven has put it in my heart, and as I’m sure it will come to pass. The eagle came from the mountain where it was bred and has its nest, and likewise Odysseus, after traveling far and suffering much, will return to take his revenge—if indeed he isn’t back already, plotting mischief for the suitors.”
“May Zeus grant it,” replied Telemachus. “If that proves to be so, I’ll make vows to you as though you were a god, even when I’m at home.”

As he spoke, he lashed his horses, and they started off at full speed through the town toward the open country. The yoke swayed on their necks, and they traveled all day long until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived, son of Ortilochus, the son of Alpheus. There they spent the night and were treated hospitably. When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, they again harnessed their horses and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court. Then Pisistratus lashed his horses on, and they flew forward readily enough. Before long they came to Pylos, and Telemachus said:

“Pisistratus, I hope you’ll promise to do what I’m about to ask you. You know our fathers were old friends, and we’re both the same age. This journey has brought us even closer together. So don’t take me past my ship—leave me there. If I go to your father’s house, he’ll try to keep me out of goodwill toward me, and I must go home at once.”

Pisistratus considered how to do as requested, and in the end he thought it best to turn his horses toward the ship and put Menelaus’s beautiful presents of gold and clothing in the stern of the vessel. Then he said, “Go aboard at once and tell your men to do the same before I can reach home to tell my father. I know how stubborn he is, and I’m sure he won’t let you go. He’ll come down here to fetch you and won’t go back without you. But he’ll be very angry.”

With this he drove his fine horses back to the city of the Pylians and soon reached his home. But Telemachus called his men together and gave his orders. “Now, my men,” he said, “get everything ready on board the ship, and let’s set out for home.”

They did as he said and went aboard. But as Telemachus was busy making prayers and sacrifices to Athena in the ship’s stern, there came to him a man from a distant country—a seer fleeing from Argos because he had killed a man. He was descended from Melampus, who used to live in Pylos, the land of sheep. Melampus had been rich and owned a great house, but was driven into exile by the great and powerful king Neleus. Neleus seized his goods and held them for a whole year, during which Melampus was imprisoned in the house of King Phylacus, in great distress of mind both because of Neleus’s daughter and because he was haunted by a great sorrow that dread Erinys had laid upon him. In the end, however, he escaped with his life, drove the cattle from Phylace to Pylos, avenged the wrong done to him, and gave Neleus’s daughter to his brother. Then he left the country and went to Argos, where he was destined to rule over many people. There he married, established himself, and had two famous sons: Antiphates and Mantius. Antiphates became father of Oicleus, and Oicleus of Amphiaraus, who was dearly loved by both Zeus and Apollo, but didn’t live to old age, for he was killed in Thebes because of a woman’s gifts. His sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus. Mantius, Melampus’s other son, was father to Polypheides and Cleitus. Eos, goddess of the dawn, enthroned in gold, carried off Cleitus for his beauty’s sake, so he might dwell among the immortals, but Apollo made Polypheides the greatest seer in the world now that Amphiaraus was dead. Polypheides quarreled with his father and went to live in Hyperesia, where he remained and prophesied for all men.

His son, Theoclymenus, was the one who now approached Telemachus as he was making drink offerings and praying in his ship. “Friend,” he said, “since I find you sacrificing in this place, I beg you by your sacrifices and by the god to whom you make them, and by your own head and those of your followers—tell me the truth and nothing but the truth. Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me also about your city and parents.”

Telemachus said, “I’ll answer you truthfully. I’m from Ithaca, and my father is Odysseus, as surely as he ever lived. But he’s come to some miserable end. That’s why I’ve taken this ship and gathered my crew, to see if I can hear any news of him, for he’s been away a long time.”

“I too am an exile,” answered Theoclymenus, “for I’ve killed a man of my own people. He has many brothers and kinsmen in Argos who have great power among the Argives. I’m fleeing to escape death at their hands, and am thus doomed to wander the earth. I’m your suppliant—take me aboard your ship so they won’t kill me, for I know they’re pursuing me.”
“I won’t refuse you,” replied Telemachus, “if you wish to join us. Come then, and in Ithaca we’ll treat you hospitably with what we have.”

At this he took Theoclymenus’s spear and laid it on the ship’s deck. He went aboard and sat in the stern, telling Theoclymenus to sit beside him. Then the men let go the hawsers. Telemachus told them to catch hold of the ropes, and they hurried to obey. They set the mast in its socket in the crossbeam, raised it and secured it with the forestays, and hoisted their white sails with ropes of twisted ox hide. Athena sent them a fair wind that blew fresh and strong to carry the ship on her course as fast as possible. So they passed by Crouni and Chalcis.

Soon the sun set and darkness covered all the land. The vessel made quick passage to Pheae and then on to Elis, where the Epeans rule. Telemachus then headed toward the flying islands, wondering within himself whether he would escape death or be taken prisoner.

Meanwhile, Odysseus and the swineherd were eating their supper in the hut, and the men ate with them. As soon as they had finished eating and drinking, Odysseus began testing the swineherd to see whether he would continue treating him kindly and ask him to stay at the station, or send him away to the city. So he said:

“Eumaeus, and all of you—tomorrow I want to go away and start begging around the town, so I won’t be more trouble to you or your men. Give me your advice, and let me have a good guide to go with me and show me the way. I’ll make the rounds of the city begging, as I must, to see if anyone will give me a drink and a piece of bread. I’d also like to go to Odysseus’s house and bring news of her husband to Queen Penelope. I could then move among the suitors and see if, out of all their abundance, they’ll give me dinner. I’d soon make them an excellent servant in all kinds of ways. Listen and believe me when I tell you that by the blessing of Hermes, who gives grace and good reputation to all men’s work, there’s no one living who would make a handier servant than I would—to put fresh wood on the fire, chop fuel, carve meat, cook, pour wine, and do all those services that poor men must do for their betters.”

The swineherd was very disturbed when he heard this. “Heaven help me,” he exclaimed, “whatever could have put such an idea into your head? If you go near the suitors, you’ll surely be destroyed, for their pride and arrogance reach the very heavens. They would never think of taking a man like you as a servant. Their servants are all young men, well-dressed, wearing good cloaks and shirts, with handsome faces and well-groomed hair. The tables are kept spotless and loaded with bread, meat, and wine. Stay where you are—you’re not in anyone’s way. I don’t mind you being here, and neither do any of the others. When Telemachus comes home, he’ll give you a shirt and cloak and send you wherever you want to go.”

Odysseus answered, “May you be as dear to the gods as you are to me, for saving me from wandering about and getting into trouble. There’s nothing worse than always being on the road. Still, when men have fallen low in the world, they’ll endure a great deal for the sake of their miserable bellies. Since you urge me to stay here and await Telemachus’s return, tell me about Odysseus’s mother and his father, whom he left on the threshold of old age when he set out for Troy. Are they still living, or are they already dead and in the house of Hades?”

“I’ll tell you all about them,” replied Eumaeus. “Laertes is still living and prays to heaven to let him die peacefully in his own house, for he’s terribly distressed about his son’s absence and also about his wife’s death, which grieved him greatly and aged him more than anything else. She came to an unhappy end through sorrow for her son—may no friend or neighbor who has been kind to me suffer such an end as she did. As long as she was still alive, though she was always grieving, I enjoyed seeing her and asking how she was, for she raised me along with her daughter Ctimene, the youngest of her children. We grew up together as boy and girl, and she treated us almost the same. When we both came of age, they sent Ctimene to Same and received a splendid dowry for her. As for me, my mistress gave me a good shirt and cloak with a pair of sandals for my feet, and sent me to work in the country, but she was just as fond of me as ever. This is all over now. Still, it has pleased heaven to bless my work in the position I now hold. I have enough to eat and drink, and can provide for any respectable stranger who comes here. But there’s no getting a kind word or deed from my mistress now, for the house has fallen into the hands of wicked people. Servants sometimes want to see their mistress and talk with her—they like to have something to eat and drink at the house, and something to take back with them to the country. This is what keeps servants content.”

Odysseus answered, “Then you must have been just a little boy, Eumaeus, when you were taken so far from your home and parents. Tell me truly: was the city where your father and mother lived sacked and pillaged, or did enemies carry you off when you were alone tending sheep or cattle, ship you here, and sell you for whatever your master paid them?”

“Stranger,” replied Eumaeus, “regarding your question: sit still, make yourself comfortable, drink your wine, and listen to me. The nights are at their longest now—there’s plenty of time for both sleeping and sitting up talking together. You shouldn’t go to bed until it’s time—too much sleep is as bad as too little. If any of the others want to go to bed, let them leave us and do so. Then they can take my master’s pigs out after breakfast in the morning. We’ll sit here eating and drinking in the hut, telling each other stories about our misfortunes. When a man has suffered much and been knocked about in the world, he takes pleasure in recalling sorrows that have long passed. So regarding your question, my story is as follows:

“You may have heard of an island called Syra that lies beyond Ortygia, where the land begins to curve around and face another direction. It’s not very heavily populated, but the soil is good, with much pasture suitable for cattle and sheep, and it abounds with wine and wheat. Famine never comes there, nor are the people plagued by sickness, but when they grow old, Apollo comes with Artemis and kills them with his painless arrows. It contains two communities, and the whole country is divided between them. My father, Ctesius son of Ormenus, a man comparable to the gods, ruled over both.

“Now some cunning traders from Phoenicia came to this place (for the Phoenicians are great sailors) in a ship they had loaded with trinkets of all kinds. There happened to be a Phoenician woman in my father’s house—very tall and beautiful, and an excellent servant. These scoundrels got hold of her one day when she was washing near their ship, seduced her, and sweet-talked her in ways no woman can resist, no matter how virtuous she may be by nature. The man who had seduced her asked who she was and where she came from, and she told him her father’s name. ‘I come from Sidon,’ she said, ‘and am daughter to Arybas, a man rolling in wealth. One day as I was coming into town from the countryside, some Taphian pirates seized me and brought me here over the sea, where they sold me to the man who owns this house, and he paid them their price for me.’
“The man who had seduced her then said, ‘Would you like to come with us to see your parents’ house and your parents themselves? They’re both alive and said to be well off.’
“‘I’ll do so gladly,’ she answered, ‘if you men will first swear a solemn oath that you’ll do me no harm along the way.’

“They all swore as she demanded, and when they had completed their oath, the woman said, ‘Be quiet now, and if any of your men meets me in the street or at the well, don’t let him speak to me, for fear someone might go and tell my master. If he suspects something, he’ll put me in prison and have all of you murdered. Keep this to yourselves—buy your merchandise as quickly as you can, and send me word when you’ve finished loading. I’ll bring as much gold as I can get my hands on, and there’s something else I can do to help pay my passage. I’m nurse to the master’s son, a funny little fellow just old enough to run around. I’ll carry him off in your ship, and you’ll get a great deal of money for him if you take him and sell him in foreign lands.’

“At this she returned to the house. The Phoenicians stayed a whole year until they had loaded their ship with precious merchandise. When they had enough cargo, they sent word to the woman. Their messenger, a very cunning fellow, came to my father’s house bringing a gold necklace strung with amber beads. While my mother and the servants were handling it, admiring it and bargaining over it, he quietly signaled to the woman and then returned to the ship. At that she took me by the hand and led me out of the house. In the front part of the house she saw tables set with cups from guests who had been feasting with my father as his attendants—these men had now all gone to a public assembly. She snatched up three cups and hid them in the folds of her dress while I followed her, knowing no better. The sun had now set and darkness covered all the land, so we hurried as fast as we could until we reached the harbor, where the Phoenician ship was moored. When they got aboard, they sailed away over the sea, taking us with them, and Zeus sent them a fair wind. We sailed six days, both night and day, but on the seventh day Artemis struck the woman and she fell heavily into the ship’s hold like a seagull dropping to the water. So they threw her overboard to the seals and fish, and I was left all sorrowful and alone. Eventually the winds and waves carried the ship to Ithaca, where Laertes traded various possessions for me, and that’s how I came to set eyes on this country.”

Odysseus answered, “Eumaeus, I’ve listened to the story of your misfortunes with the deepest interest and sympathy, but Zeus has given you good as well as evil. Despite everything, you have a good master who sees that you always have enough to eat and drink, and you lead a good life, while I’m still wandering from city to city, begging my way.”

So they talked, and they had only a little time left for sleep, for dawn was soon coming. Meanwhile, Telemachus and his crew were nearing land, so they lowered the sails, took down the mast, and rowed the ship into the harbor. They dropped their mooring stones and made fast the hawsers, then got out on the seashore, mixed their wine, and got dinner ready. As soon as they had eaten and drunk enough, Telemachus said, “Take the ship on to the town, but leave me here, for I want to check on the herdsmen at one of my farms. In the evening, when I’ve seen everything I need to see, I’ll come down to the city, and tomorrow morning I’ll give you all a good dinner with meat and wine in return for your service.”
Then Theoclymenus said, “And what’s to become of me, my dear young friend? To whose house, among all your leading men, should I go? Or shall I go straight to your own house and to your mother?”

“At any other time,” replied Telemachus, “I would invite you to my own house, for you’d find no lack of hospitality. At the present moment, however, you wouldn’t be comfortable there, since I’ll be away and my mother won’t see you. She doesn’t often show herself even to the suitors, but sits at her loom weaving in an upper chamber, keeping out of their way. But I can tell you whose house you can go to—I mean Eurymachus, son of Polybus, who is held in the highest regard by everyone in Ithaca. He’s by far the best man and the most persistent suitor among all those courting my mother and trying to take Odysseus’s place. Zeus alone in heaven, however, knows whether they’ll come to a bad end before the marriage takes place.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right—a hawk, Apollo’s messenger. It held a dove in its talons, and as it tore the feathers off, they fell to the ground midway between Telemachus and the ship. At this Theoclymenus called him aside and grasped his hand. “Telemachus,” he said, “that bird didn’t fly on your right without being sent there by some god. As soon as I saw it, I knew it was an omen. It means you’ll remain in power and that no house in Ithaca will be more royal than your own.”
“I hope it proves true,” answered Telemachus. “If it does, I’ll show you such goodwill and give you so many gifts that everyone who meets you will congratulate you.”

Then he said to his friend Piraeus, “Piraeus, son of Clytius, you’ve shown yourself most willing to serve me of all those who accompanied me to Pylos. I want you to take this stranger to your own house and entertain him hospitably until I can come for him.”
Piraeus answered, “Telemachus, you may stay away as long as you like, but I’ll look after him for you, and he’ll find no lack of hospitality.”

As he spoke, he went aboard and told the others to do the same and loose the hawsers. So they took their places in the ship. But Telemachus strapped on his sandals and took a long, sturdy spear with a sharp bronze point from the ship’s deck. Then they loosed the hawsers, pushed the ship away from shore, and headed toward the city as they had been told, while Telemachus strode away as fast as he could until he reached the homestead where his countless herds of swine were feeding, and where lived the excellent swineherd, who was such a devoted servant to his master.
